# Methods before long reads

::: {.callout-warning}
## First draft
Written from `research/04-technology-arc.yml` and not yet reviewed by a second
reader.
Eighteen of this chapter's sources were read as abstracts rather than as full
text, more than in any other chapter.
:::

Every claim about alternative splicing has an assay behind it, and the assay
fixes what kind of claim it can be. A method that measures a length can
establish that a transcript is discontinuous without establishing that the
discontinuity is regulated. A method that counts junctions can establish
prevalence, and cannot establish which junctions occurred in the same molecule.

The sections below follow that constraint rather than the chronology, taking one
generation of method at a time with the specific thing it could not reach.

## Electron microscopy and a split transcript {#sec-1977}

Splicing was established by a physical measurement rather than by a sequence.
Berget, Moore and Sharp located adenovirus hexon mRNA on the viral genome by
examining RNA-DNA hybrids in the electron microscope [@berget1977spliced].

The inference rested on a length of unpaired RNA. About 160 nucleotides at the
mRNA's 5' end failed to pair with the single-stranded DNA encoding the rest of
the message [@berget1977spliced].

A second group reached the same place by a different hybridisation geometry.
R-loops formed between viral DNA and unfractionated polysomal RNA resolved
three short segments from distant map positions, fused into one leader of 150
to 200 nucleotides [@chow1977amazing].

Two unlike physical assays put the same segments at the same coordinates.
Neither could give a sequence or an exact splice boundary, so the claim they
licensed was the narrow one that a transcript can be discontinuous.

## cDNA clones and a regulated choice {#sec-regulated}

Immunoglobulin was one route to the next claim. The membrane and secreted forms
of the mu heavy chain travel on two different mRNAs, one of 2.7 and one of 2.4
kilobases. That came from restriction mapping and sequencing of cDNA clones
taken from a tumour making both chains [@rogers1980twomrnas].

Calcitonin was the other, and its authors drew the general conclusion.
Alternative processing of calcitonin gene transcripts yields distinct mRNAs
with different tissue distributions. They proposed this as a strategy:
developmental regulation of RNA processing as a way of increasing the diversity
of neuroendocrine gene expression [@amara1982alternative].

The same group later made the methodological argument explicit. Cloning
together with processing analysis could reach a complex neurobiological system
with no prior structural or biological information about the product it would
find [@rosenfeld1983production]. The method had become a way of discovering
biology rather than confirming it.

## RT-PCR and one locus at a time {#sec-low-throughput}

For roughly two decades after that, measuring splicing meant one locus and one
gene. RT-PCR was the conventional approach, and retrospectives written three
decades later still name it as such [@park2018expanding].

Solution hybridisation with nuclease protection was the more quantitative
alternative to RNA blot analysis. Its own practitioners recorded the catch,
which was that at a locus making several mRNAs by alternative splicing the
protected-fragment pattern from a uniformly labelled cRNA probe became hard to
interpret [@nucleaseprotection1989solution].

An assay can be sensitive without being diagnostic. In the S1 nuclease
configuration best suited to demonstrating a splice, unspliced and spliced RNA
both protect the probe across the junction. The assay was reported as not
diagnostic, and needed an RNase H pre-digestion to become one
[@rnaseh1987s1artefact].

The deeper limitation was combinatorial, and it outlasted the era. As late as
2010, authors building a single-molecule splicing readout opened by stating it
plainly: studying linked regulation of multiple splice sites within one gene,
in transcripts such as Dscam, required new approaches
[@conze2010singlemolecule]. The arithmetic in @sec-dscam is precisely what a
bulk assay cannot report. Inclusion frequencies measured one exon at a time are
compatible with combinations across molecules that contradict each other.

## ESTs and the first genome-scale numbers {#sec-est-era}

Expressed sequence tags made a genome-scale count possible, and the counts did
not settle.

Spliced alignment of EST contigs in 1999 put alternative splicing at 35 per
cent of known human genes. Most of the detected variation sat in 5'
untranslated regions rather than in coding sequence [@mironov1999frequent].

A different EST comparison a year later gave 38 per cent, over 7,867
non-redundant mRNAs of which 3,011 carried an alternative form. Its event
spectrum was roughly 70 per cent exon deletions against 30 per cent insertions
[@brett2000estcomparison].

Mapping roughly 2.1 million human mRNA and EST sequences onto the draft genome
raised the estimate again, to 42 per cent of human genes or more
[@modrek2001genomewide].

Then the dependence was demonstrated rather than suspected. With sufficient EST
coverage, nearly every gene examined showed some alternative form. Requiring a
variant above five per cent with statistical support collapsed the yield to 17
to 28 per cent of genes [@kan2002selecting]. One dataset therefore supports two
defensible numbers, and the threshold is the whole difference between them.

By 2004 the counter-argument was in print. Cassette exons seen only in EST
databases differed systematically from cross-species conserved ones, and a
significant portion were argued to be aberrant splicing rather than regulated
isoforms [@sorek2004howprevalent]. The headline number was a function of
library depth and of the threshold applied to it, and @fig-prevalence shows
what that does to a decade of published estimates.

## Arrays and the designed survey {#sec-arrays}

Arrays moved the measurement from discovery to a designed survey. Junction
microarrays monitored every exon-exon junction in more than 10,000 multi-exon
human genes across 52 tissues and cell lines. Their authors concluded that at
least 74 per cent of human multi-exon genes are alternatively spliced
[@johnson2003genomewide].

Combining exon-body probes with splice-junction probes on one platform made
tissue-specific alternative splicing quantitative for thousands of exons in
mouse tissues [@pan2004revealing]. One human compendium designed arrays carrying
probes for 203,672 exons and for 178,351 junctions, across 17,939 genes
[@castle2008differential]. That coverage is large, and it is fixed before the
experiment begins.

Arrays had a structural blind spot by event class, because alternative 5' and 3'
splice sites shift the message by a region often too small to interrogate with a
probe [@wang2008alternative]. The splicing index, on which most array splicing
calls rested, assumes that a gene's exons move together when its transcription
changes. That assumption was shown not to hold on real exon-array data,
substantially inflating the apparent number of alternatively spliced exons for
technical reasons [@gaidatzis2009overestimation].

## RNA-seq and the near-universal estimate {#sec-rnaseq-arrives}

RNA-seq removed the design step, and the 2008 mouse reference datasets rested on
41 to 52 million mapped 25-base reads from poly(A)-selected RNA of three
tissues. They yielded a junction census of about 145,000 distinct splices, with
roughly 3,500 genes expressing one or more alternate internal splice
[@mortazavi2008mapping].

A parallel human study reported 94,241 splice junctions from two cell lines, of
which only 4,096 were previously unidentified. Exon skipping was the most
prevalent form of alternative splicing [@sultan2008globalview]. The companion
study behind the near-universality claim sequenced 12 to 29 million 32-base
cDNA fragments per sample, from ten human tissues and five mammary epithelial
or breast cancer cell lines [@wang2008alternative].

The most-quoted figure needs its provenance attached, because the claim that
about 95 per cent of multi-exon human genes are alternatively spliced is not a
pure RNA-seq result. Its source states that the estimate came from combining
mRNA-Seq with EST and cDNA sequence data [@pan2008deepsurveying].

The companion number is an extrapolation over a stated denominator. Multi-exon
genes, 94 per cent of all RefSeq genes, were binned by read coverage and a
sigmoid was fitted. The asymptote lands near 98 to 100 per cent of multi-exon
genes [@wang2008alternative].

The same paper carries a more conservative figure bounded by a threshold.
Requiring a minor isoform to exceed 15 per cent of the gene's output in at least
one sample gives 92 per cent of multi-exon genes. Those authors rescale that to
about 86 per cent of all human genes [@wang2008alternative].

![Ten years of estimates of how many human genes are alternatively spliced. The
denominators differ, the abundance thresholds differ, and two of the values are
extrapolations rather than counts. The spread is the subject, and reading the
column as a rising trend reads nine questions as
one.](../figures/prevalence-estimates.svg){#fig-prevalence width=100%}

What that figure counts, and under which conditions, is taken up in
@sec-how-functional.

## Short reads could not reconstruct a molecule {#sec-short-read-limit}

The full-length reconstruction problem was named in the EST era. The
high-throughput methods of the day returned detailed information about short
fragments only. Recovering whole isoform structures from a
fragment mixture was posed as a separate inference task
[@xing2004multiassembly].

Short reads inherited that problem, and the Cufflinks authors state the
limitation in their own opening paragraph: assembly and abundance estimation are
hard because a read generally cannot be attributed to one isoform
[@trapnell2010transcript]. They also record what they had done instead in
earlier work, which was to quantify genes without allocating reads among
alternative isoforms, while still reporting evidence that several forms were
co-expressed [@trapnell2010transcript].

A community assessment put numbers on the cost. Best-method transcript-level
recovery fell as the genome got more complex. It ran from 56 to 59 per cent of
spliced protein-coding transcripts in *C. elegans*, to 43 per cent in *D.
melanogaster*, to 21 per cent in *H. sapiens* [@steijger2013assessment]. The
same assessment separated the two failure modes and found both active. For most
transcripts not every constituent exon was detected, and even where all exons
were reported the methods frequently could not link them into a complete isoform
[@steijger2013assessment].

Read length buys assignment, and the amount is measurable. Comparing two
Illumina paired-end libraries from the same cell line, 25.04 per cent of
assignable 75-base reads matched exactly one annotated isoform, against 32.98
per cent at 262 bases [@cho2014highresolution].

Depth does not substitute for length, since reads that map to several places
stay common however deeply a library is sequenced, so more data does not remove
that uncertainty [@zheng2022nonidentifiability]. The limitation
is formal as well as practical. Different sets of transcript abundances can
generate the observed reads with equal likelihood, so the maximum-likelihood
answer is not unique, and the underlying true expression cannot be determined
from the reads [@zheng2022nonidentifiability].

The field's response was to stop asking for full-length structures. Event-based
tools count reads over particular exons and junctions and report a
percent-spliced-in value, measuring one decision instead of solving for the
whole molecule [@park2018expanding]. That is where PSI comes from, and
@sec-psi gives what it costs.

Thirty years of method development had converged on a measurement that
answers a smaller question very well. The smaller question leaves out the
molecule, and getting it back took a longer read, which is @sec-one-molecule.
